full_judgment:
18. Mr. Rokonnuddin Mahmood, the learned Advocate for petitioner in Writ Petition No.767 of 1991 thereafter referred to the decision in the case of Moazzem Hossain Chowdhury Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 43 DLR 186 to show that when the District Magistrate passed order of detention on the ground enumerated in section 2(1)(i) of the Special Powers Act, the order of detention is void ab initio. that the legislature in enacting the Special Powers Act has not empowered the District Magistrate and Additional District Magistrate (under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act) to make any order of preventive detention on the grounds mentioned in clauses (i) and (ii) of section 2(1) in respect of which the Government alone can make any order of preventive detention of any person. He thereafter, submits that if in the aforesaid case reported in 43 DLR /86 the District Magistrate who had passed the void order of detention, also notified in the official Gazette under section 7(b) of the said Act directing the detenu to appear before a specified officer, at a specified place and within a period specified in the order, if the said person failed to comply with such direction, if the police after investigation submitted charge sheet against such detenu and if the relevant Special Tribunal took cognizance of the said offence under section 7(b) of the said Act, this Court in exercise of its writ jurisdiction under Article 102(2)(a)(ii)( certiorari) of the Constitution would have to declare the proceeding pending before the said Special Tribunal under section 7(b) of the said Act to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect (provided, of course, that the detenu did not remain fugitive from law and justice and surrendered to the jurisdiction of the Special Tribunal in question). Mr. Hasan Ariff, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Government was candid enough to concede that by now it is well settled that in such circumstances where the initial order of detention is void ab initio. the proceeding under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act would also be without lawful authority and of no legal effect in view of the several decisions, such as, the cases of Sultan Ali Naghiana Vs. Nur Hussain, AIR 1949(Lahore) 13/ (Full Bench), Dr. MO Ghani Vs. ANM Mahmmod, PLD /966 Supreme Court 802, Director of Public Prosecutions Vs. Head (1958) 1 All ER 679 (686). In the case of Sultan Ali Naghiana, AIR /949 (Lahore) 131 (155) Munir, C] delivering judgment of the Full Bench observed: 

 20. We will presently show that when the order of detention is nullity and void ab initio the subsequent notification in the Gazette under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 also becomes a nullity and void ab initio and the consequential proceeding before the Special Tribunal under the said section 7(b) of the said Act for non-compliance of such null and void order becomes illegal and without lawful authority and that in the instant case the order. of detention is void ab initio because the detaining authority did not at all have before it "the jurisdiction facts" i.e. any report or reports and materials to enable the detaining authority to form its opinion that the person concerned should be detained for preventing him from acting in prejudicial manner and also because the involvement grounds given for preventive detention do not come within the meaning of the expression "prejudicial act" as defined in section 2(1) of the Special Powers 10 Act. In this context in those two Habeas Corpus Writ Petitions we relied upon the following portions of the celebrated decision in the case of Abdul Latif Mirza Vs. Bangladesh, 31 DLR(AD) 1 (which are based on several other important decisions of the Supreme Court of Pakistan referred to by the Appellate Division in that decision) : 

 If there was any statutory provision of appeal or revision in this case for setting aside the proceedings, then the question whether any equally efficacious adequate alternative remedy is available to the petitioner would act as a bar to move this Court under Article 102(2) of the Constitution. In the instant case the inherent jurisdiction of the High Court Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot he said to be an alternative remedy to this court's writ jurisdiction under Article 102(2) of the Constitution. In the case of Nagina Silk Mills, Lyallpur Vs. Income Tax Officer, A Ward, Lyallpur, 15 DLR (SC) 181 it was observed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan: 

 We have found in the judgments of the said two writ petitions that the orders of detention made against the two detenus under section 3 of the Special Powers Act read with the grounds of detention communicated to the detenus under section 8(1) of the Special Powers Act were made arbitrarily for collateral purpose in colourable exercise of power and that none of the grounds of detention communicated to the accused petitioners comes within the mischief of the expression "prejudicial act" as defined in section 2(f) of the Special Powers Act. These grounds of detention were undisputedly and admittedly not based on any report or material whatsoever to enable the detaining authority to make the order of detention within the meaning of section 3 of the Special Powers Act. Since the detaining authority is curtailing the liberty of person of a citizen by detaining him on the preventive detention, it is undisputedly exercising quasi judicial authority. To curtail fundamental right of personal liberty of a citizen which is enshrined in Article 32 read with Article 33 of the Constitution, it is essential that the detaining authority must have reports and materials, that is 'jurisdictional facts' for exercising of its power to detain the detenu under section 3 read with section 8 of the Special Powers Act (see Abdul Latif Mirza, 31 DLR (AD) 1). The question of "jurisdictional facts" giving power to an authority or tribunal to exercise statutory power has been dealt with by HKR Wade in his book "Administrative Law" (4th Edition) (2nd impression) (1979) at page 238-243. In the book "Principles of Administrative Law". by MP Jain and SN Jain (4th Edition) at page 538 it has been observed.
